newsitem.title: USA: Muni buyers seek rehearing of appeals court ruling.
newsitem.headline: Muni buyers seek rehearing of appeals court ruling.

text.p: Warning that the ruling has "rattled" the legal and muni finance community, investors asked a U.S. appeals court to reconsider a finding that IRS can bill investors for interest on muni bonds found taxable.

"The panel has dealt a crippling blow to the congressional purpose of encouraging state, municipal, educational and public benefit projects," lawyers for Harbor Bancorp and other investors said in 14-page filing with the Ninth U.S. Court of Appeals.

A three-judge panel June 10 upheld an earlier U.S. Tax Court ruling that Internal Revenue Service acted correctly in declaring taxable $30 million in bonds sold by the Riverside County, Calif., Housing Authority to build two facilities.
The Whitewater Garden apartments project was never built and the Ironwood project was constructed under another name -- but not with bond proceeds.

Both deals were rushed to market Dec 31, 1985, by New York City underwriter Matthews & Wright to beat a new federal curb on "arbitrage" profits. That firm's broker-dealer license was later revoked by the Securities and Exchange Commission.
SEC had concluded that the closings were "shams" because no money actually changed hands.
The three-judge panel earlier this month said IRS acted properly in trying to bill investors even though they were unaware of Matthews & Wright's behind-the-scenes strategy.
The panel conceded that the investors' arguments were "plausible," but deferred to IRS because the Service presented a "permissible reading" of an admittedly "ambiguous" part of the U.S Tax Code.

But Bryan Cave, the law firm representing bondholders, argued in its filing late yesterday that "ambiguous provisions of the tax code should be construed in favor of the taxpayer, not ... the Commissioner of Internal Revenue."
It warned that the "astonishing" June 10 ruling will have a "profound impact on the entire tax-exempt finance community."

Some issuers will withdraw from the bond market because of the risks, the filing says. Others will find it necessary to pay for "massive, costly investigations" into the bond firms handling their offerings, the filing adds.
